_what: Camera solved from est-living/Timothy Kaye plate gh-11 (Garden House, McCluskey Studio) by the fSpy method, re-implemented as arithmetic. See NOTES.md step 2.

solution.scale_source: SP01 Michelle bar stool, 915 mm hoop apex over its own back feet -> 1596 mm; island -> 1466; oak bank at ceiling 3400 -> 1379; trimmed to 1480 by the two appliance widths (oven 803 vs 762 published, fridge 897 vs 914).
solution._rot_z_note: Blender XYZ euler with rot_x=90 leaves the camera looking along +Y, so rot_z rotates that: forward = (-sin g, cos g, 0). To look along (-0.5128, -0.8586) the answer is g = 180 - 30.85 = 149.15 deg, NOT -30.85. The yaw off the kitchen wall is still 30.85 deg; only the euler encoding differs.

checks.orthogonality: the two axis directions come out 90.02 deg apart. Nothing forced this - the two vanishing points were fitted from different objects (cabinetry vs glazing+island) and the principal point was assumed at image mid-width. A wrong horizon or a wrong focal length would not land on 90.
checks.against_the_tutorial: 3D Shaker's fSpy solve of this same photo put its camera at rotation Z = -30.302 deg. Mine, solved independently from sub-pixel edge fits, is -30.85 deg. 0.55 deg apart.
checks.camera_height: 1379 mm here vs the 1.5 m they typed. They typed a round number because the box 'felt too big'; this is derived from the ratio of two horizontal lines on one plane (oak cabinet top vs its plinth) and is independent of focal length.

assumptions: the frame's verticals are vertical, so the camera is level and the principal point lies on the horizon (shift lens or a perspective correction in post)
no horizontal shift: principal point x = image mid-width
ceiling height 3400 mm - the one number that is asserted rather than measured; camera height scales with it
